text: 🌊 The glass salp: a species that waited twenty years for a name In Monterey Bay, between 280 and 2,200 metres down, drifts a transparent barrel that spent two decades turning up in MBARI's records without a name. Larry Madin of Woods Hole and MBARI has now described it in Marine Biodiversity as Vitreosalpa gemini — a new species and a new genus. It is the first salp known to spend its whole life in the twilight and midnight zones: relatives stay near the surface, some migrating to 800 metres but not living there. Its body is watery and slow, its metabolism lower than that of surface kin, and it feeds on detritus and single-celled protozoans rather than on living phytoplankton. The name marks two traits: glassy transparency and twin embryos. The chains of clones towed by a solitary individual — up to twenty have been seen — breed sexually, each producing two offspring at once, a rare trick among salps that may double reproductive output where relatives are scarce. Video: MBARI #ocean @science

Crystals can repeat with 2-, 3-, 4- or 6-fold symmetry. This alloy came back with five. The rule is geometric. A crystal repeats by translation, and no arrangement of identical units can turn five times and still close up; regular pentagons tile a floor only by leaving gaps. The pattern showed six five-fold, ten three-fold and fifteen two-fold axes, with spots as sharp as any crystal's, and no lattice to index them. The phase was aluminium with 14 atomic per cent manganese, cooled fast enough to trap it, in grains up to two micrometres across. It is metastable and forms from the melt by a first-order transition. The authors' wording is the careful part: orientational order without translational order. What broke was not the measurement but the definition, which now covers any solid with a sharp diffraction pattern. Source: Shechtman, Blech, Gratias & Cahn, Physical Review Letters (1984) · doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.53.1951

🔬 Tiny chip generates UV light where bulky sources couldn't A Harvard-led team has built a microscopic photonic device that produces roughly 120 times more ultraviolet power than previous comparable designs. The trick: instead of pushing UV light through lossy on-chip channels, the device converts red light into UV light inside a thin-film lithium niobate chip, using a process called frequency upconversion. The work, published in Nature Communications, positions lithium niobate as a compact platform for powerful UV sources, with potential uses from smaller quantum computers to ultra-precise atomic clocks. The strongest number: about 120 times more UV power than earlier comparable devices. The team notes there are nonlinear effects in the device they don't fully understand yet. #UVphotonics #LithiumNiobate #QuantumComputing @science

🧠 Neuralink has FDA clearance for its decisive N1 trial On 25 November the FDA allowed Neuralink to launch the LINK Pivotal Study — the first pivotal trial of an implantable brain-computer interface in the United States. It tests safety and effectiveness in people with severe paralysis from ALS: the N1 chip, 1,024 electrodes on 64 threads, is placed by the R1 robot, and a decoder turns motor-cortex activity into cursor motion. Behind it are more than thirty participants in the US, Canada and the UK; in earlier reports people reached up to 40 words per minute by thought. The clearance covers a study, not a sale: the implant stays investigational. A January 2026 report notes performance varies between patients, and in the first participant some threads partly retracted from the tissue. Critics, among them Surjo Soekadar of Charité, say the company discloses little about complications and that non-invasive eye tracking would spare some patients a risky operation. Video: Neuralink #BCI @science

The ring around the black hole in M87 is 42 microarcseconds across, give or take three. That number belongs to the instrument, not to the galaxy: eight radio stations, recording at a wavelength of 1.3 millimetres, combined into a single aperture as wide as the Earth by very long baseline interferometry. The image that came out is an asymmetric bright ring with a dark centre, brighter on one side, with a flux ratio above 10 to 1 between ring and shadow. At the distance of the Moon, 42 microarcseconds would span about eight centimetres. A credit card left on the lunar surface is the smallest thing that eye could resolve. The ring is light from behind the hole, bent around it; the darkness inside is the shadow of the horizon, and the asymmetry is gas orbiting near the speed of light. From the ring's size the collaboration weighed the hole at 6.5 billion Suns. Source: EHT Collaboration, ApJ Letters (2019) · doi.org/10.3847/2041-8213/ab0ec7

🐝 Wasps have their own biological Face ID — remarkably similar to ours. Researchers have identified specialized neurons in the brains of northern paper wasps that respond to individual facial features of other wasps. Despite having only around a million neurons, these insects use a facial recognition mechanism strikingly similar to that found in primates. It helps them maintain social hierarchies without constantly fighting. The study suggests that evolution independently developed similar neural solutions in insects and mammals, although their mechanisms are not identical. Perhaps intelligence is not just about brain size, but how efficiently neurons are organized. #Science #Neuroscience #Evolution #Biology #Intelligence https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cell.2026.10.052

🧬 GPT‑6 designed proteins that bind their targets OpenAI has posted a preprint: the GPT‑6 family designs a protein's 3D shape and its amino-acid sequence using only reasoning and ordinary code — with no specialised biology models at the generation stage. In lab tests with Onava, proteins built from GPT‑6.2's designs showed evidence of binding across five targets, and redesigned antibodies kept binding. An internal research model matched or beat specialised models on many design tasks. The authors' own caveat: the campaign relied on Boltz‑2, OpenDDE and ESMFold2 to filter candidates. The intrinsic ability is comparable to specialised models at two stages — backbone generation (RFdiffusion) and sequence redesign (ProteinMPNN) — plus a memorisation caveat in structure-to-sequence tests. This is not "AI discovered a drug". The shift is elsewhere: protein design stops being a separate discipline and becomes a task for a general-purpose model. #biotech #AI #OpenAI @science

A planet about the mass of Jupiter circles 51 Pegasi every 4.23 days. A year there is shorter than a school week. Nothing in our own system comes close. Mercury, the fastest planet here, takes 88 days; the new companion sits about eight million kilometres from its star, well inside Mercury's orbit, where a gas giant should not survive. Its temperature is above 1,300 K. The detection is a wobble, not a picture. Since April 1994 the Geneva group had been reading radial velocities of 142 G and K dwarfs to about 13 metres per second, and one star's lines slid back and forth on a 4.23-day cycle. The authors offered two readings: a giant that migrated inward, or a brown dwarf stripped of its outer layers. The search was built for stars like the Sun with planets like Jupiter in orbits like ours. It found the opposite, and the field never went back. Source: Mayor & Queloz, Nature (1995) · doi.org/10.1038/378355a0

Mathematicians are currently examining a 17-million-line proof of the Riemann Hypothesis, generated with the help of Claude (consisting of 175,187 files verified using Lean and Mathlib). To make sense of the solution, they created a visualization in the form of a map—which proved to be a huge help. 😂 But I’d like everyone to consider something. Many "naive carbon-based lifeforms" still claim, "I’ll just check every single line of code the AI ​​writes." But what happens when the AI ​​dumps N million lines of code on you, and when you ask, "Bro, how does this actually work?" it replies, "Elementary, my dear Watson—here’s a visualization for you!"? 😂 Let’s be honest: trying to understand the inner workings through manual inspection is, in a sense, a dead end. A mere mortal simply cannot grasp it—at least not within any reasonable timeframe. We need formal verification methods capable of handling this level of complexity to ensure correctness. Mathematicians at least have Lean—a formal tool for verification. Similar tools are also needed for business software, where logic is often fuzzy. Yet, by 2027, we could easily end up with a "superintelligent jellyfish" of code—the result of letting a swarm of AI agents run wild. bosnadev.com/lab/riemann/app
